title: What Oracle Infrastructure Teams Should Prepare before AI Agents Arrive
summary: Oracle AI World showed where Oracle is taking AI agents. What Oracle infrastructure teams should prepare now, from performance and dev/test to recovery.
body_markdown:
### Summary


Oracle AI World showed Oracle building toward AI agents that work directly on database data. At the event, many of the Oracle professionals we spoke with are exploring what upgrading to Oracle AI Database 26ai would mean for their environments. That evaluation window is the time to make sure the infrastructure can keep performance consistent, speed up dev/test, recover reliably, and evolve without another disruptive refresh.


Agentic AI was a major theme at Oracle AI World 2026, with Oracle emphasizing how AI agents can work closer to enterprise data while maintaining security and governance. Building on the introduction of[Oracle AI Database 26ai](https://blog.everpuredata.com/products/data-platform-oracle-ai-database-26ai/) in 2025, Oracle demonstrated how its converged database architecture brings together vector search, Graph RAG, document intelligence, and analytics alongside traditional transactional workloads. Oracle AI Database Private Agent Factory further supports this direction by providing a no-code framework for building agents that can securely access and act on enterprise data. Oracle’s argument was that the most useful AI will be the one that knows your business, and for most enterprises, a large share of that business already lives in Oracle.


The conversations on the show floor were more practical. The Oracle teams we talked with at our booth are evaluating Oracle AI Database 26ai, and the questions they brought were about problems they already deal with: keeping performance predictable, modernizing without another round of disruption, controlling cost, and limiting operational risk. Agents make each of those harder, because an agent that runs around the clock against production data adds load nobody planned for, needs realistic copies of production to be tested against, and introduces new ways for data to go wrong.


That makes the evaluation period the right time to settle the infrastructure questions agents will eventually force while the answers are still cheap to act on and before an application team connects the first agent to a production database.


## **Settle the storage roadmap before the Oracle AI Database 26ai upgrade**


An Oracle AI Database 26ai upgrade is already a project with its own round of testing, and the size of that round depends on how much sits on top of the database. We’ve written about how[the operational burden of a database estate](https://blog.everpuredata.com/products/operational-burden-of-the-database-estate/) grows with the number of things that depend on it rather than with the number of databases. An instance that served three applications two years ago now serves those applications plus an analytics pipeline and an internal API, and each of them adds a path to revalidate the next time someone patches or upgrades the instance. In the[Everpure “State of Database Infrastructure 2026](https://www.everpuredata.com/resources/type-a/state-of-database-infrastructure.html) ” research conducted with Vanson Bourne, infrastructure leaders estimated that their database teams spend nearly a fifth of their working time validating and rechecking systems after migrations and updates.


Agents extend that pattern faster than application teams ever did because an agent is quick to stand up and its access pattern comes from a prompt and a task rather than from a developer writing and tuning a query. A team in finance can connect an agent to an Oracle schema, and from the database team’s point of view, a new consumer is now issuing queries nobody load-tested at hours nobody planned for.


In “[The Oracle Cost That Never Shows Up on the Invoice](https://blog.everpuredata.com/perspectives/the-oracle-cost-that-never-shows-up/) ,” we argued that the most expensive part of running Oracle is everything built around it over the years, from backup jobs and failover runbooks to refresh scripts and monitoring. Agents add to that operating model, and every process they come to depend on is one more thing that has to keep working the next time the infrastructure underneath changes.


A storage migration is the change that breaks most of those processes at once. It means rebuilding backup jobs, failover procedures, monitoring, and automation at the same moment the team is working through a 26ai upgrade and learning how agents behave in production. Everpure™[Evergreen® architecture](https://www.everpuredata.com/knowledge/what-is-evergreen-architecture.html) decouples storage maintenance from Oracle operations. Controllers, software, and even protocols upgrade nondisruptively while production databases keep running, and the processes built around Oracle keep working through hardware changes. For a team still evaluating 26ai, that takes the storage refresh off the critical path, so the timing of the upgrade can follow the business case for the database instead of the replacement date on the arrays.


## **Performance has to hold for existing and emerging workloads on the same arrays**


Before Oracle AI World, we looked at[how Oracle AI Database 26ai changes the workload on storage](https://blog.everpuredata.com/news-events/born-to-run-pure-storage-platform-for-oracle/) . HNSW vector indexes put vector reads and writes on the same arrays that serve OLTP, embeddings grow tablespaces without growing row counts, True Cache adds sustained read throughput, and[RAG](https://www.everpuredata.com/knowledge/what-is-retrieval-augmented-generation.html) pipelines arrive in bursts alongside steady transactions. Agents make that mix harder to predict. People using an application generate load that roughly follows the business day, which is why so many Oracle shops still run backups, statistics gathering, and batch jobs overnight. An agent working through a multistep task can issue a long run of retrieval queries in quick succession, retry when a result looks incomplete, and keep going at 3am because a scheduled job started it.


For infrastructure teams, that moves the performance question from peak capacity toward predictability under contention. The useful test is whether latency for the transactional workload holds while vector search, agent retrieval, and an RMAN backup all run at the same time, since that combination stops being unusual once agents reach production. Quality-of-service controls that keep one consumer from crowding out another matter more here than headline throughput, and so does being able to see which workload is driving latency when it moves. A sizing exercise built on the team’s own AWR data, like the one in the Everpure[Oracle AI Database 26ai readiness assessment](https://blog.everpuredata.com/purely-technical/unlocking-oracle-ai-database-26ai/) , is a better starting point than a generic guide when the workload is about to change shape.


Sizing for that mix is also where much of the cost gets decided. In[one recent Everpure assessment](https://blog.everpuredata.com/purely-technical/unlocking-oracle-ai-database-26ai/) , a prospect expected to need 200TB of storage for an Oracle upgrade and turned out to need 18TB of primary data because a legacy ASM High Redundancy configuration was keeping three copies of everything. Getting the sizing right before a 26ai upgrade keeps that budget from going to capacity the database never needed.


## **Testing agents and upgrades takes more copies of production**


Few teams will want to point a new agent at a production Oracle database without first watching what it does against realistic data, which usually means a recent, full-sized copy of production. The same goes for a 26ai upgrade, which most teams will want to rehearse more than once against current data before they schedule it.


Teams will need many of these copies over time because every new agent, every revision of an existing agent’s instructions, and every upgrade rehearsal is a reason for another round of testing.


This brings our earlier point about refresh processes back into focus. In plenty of Oracle environments, refreshing a full test database still takes a weekend and a change ticket, which is manageable once a quarter and unworkable when it has to happen every time an agent changes. Everpure snapshots can create a full-sized clone of a production database in seconds, use almost no additional capacity, and leave the source database untouched. The whole process can be scripted through a REST API that stays the same across hardware generations. With that in place, retesting an agent after each revision becomes a scheduled job that runs alongside the rest of the team’s automation.


## **Recovery has to plan for a mistake an agent was allowed to make**


At Oracle AI World, Oracle introduced a new top tier of its Maximum Availability Architecture, with failover in under three seconds and zero data loss, which covers the failures most recovery plans were written for. Agents add a different kind of failure. An agent with legitimate write access can update the wrong rows, apply a change twice, or act on stale instructions, and replication will carry those changes faithfully to every standby. When something goes wrong in those cases, recovery looks different from a hardware failure or a ransomware attack. The team needs to find when the bad change started and roll back the affected data quickly, while keeping the legitimate transactions that came after it.


Oracle’s own tools, including Flashback and RMAN, remain the first line for that kind of logical recovery, and the infrastructure underneath determines how fast and how far back a team can go. Frequent, space-efficient snapshots give DBAs more recovery points to choose from, and fast clones let them bring up a copy alongside production to compare data before deciding what to roll back. Everpure[SafeMode™ Snapshots](http://purestorage.com/solutions/cyber-resilience/ransomware/safemode.html) add recovery points that can’t be deleted or encrypted even with compromised administrator credentials. That protection matters even more as agents bring new identities and credentials into the estate. But[configured protection alone doesn’t prove recovery outcomes](https://blog.everpuredata.com/perspectives/your-database-is-fine-can-you-prove-it/) ; teams also need to verify that recovery requirements remain achievable as the environment changes. Snapshot schedules and protection groups can each be configured correctly, and the only way to know they still cover everything the database depends on after agents arrive is to test recovery against the[RPO and RTO](https://blog.everpuredata.com/purely-technical/rto-vs-rpo-whats-the-difference/) the business expects.


## **Use the Oracle AI Database 26ai evaluation to test the infrastructure too**


The teams in the best position a year from now will be the ones that used their 26ai evaluation to test the infrastructure as well as the database. In practice, that means confirming the storage can be upgraded without another migration, measuring how the transactional workload behaves alongside vector search and agent retrieval, settling how test copies of production get created and refreshed, and running a recovery drill that assumes an authorized agent made a bad change. Each of those is easier to work through now, while agents are still in pilots, than after they’ve become dependencies nobody can turn off.
